title: Refined OJ Attacks: Tight Complexity for Rank Decoding Problems and Their Cryptographic Implications
authors: Yongcheng Song, Rongmao Chen, Xinyi Huang, Jiang Zhang, and Chao Lin
abstract:
The Rank Decoding (RD) problem lies at the core of rank-based cryptography. To enable efficient constructions, several variants have been introduced, notably the Non-Homogeneous RD (NHRD) problem and the Blockwise RD (BRD) problem. The \emph{quantum} security of these systems is currently considered to be determined by the complexity of combinatorial attacks such as AGHT, PRR, and Ourivski--Johansson (OJ) attacks. However, for the OJ attack, the modeling, soundness, and relative complexities remain poorly understood, particularly for the NHRD and BRD variants, thereby limiting confidence in security claims and hindering the design of compact schemes.

In this work, we refine the modelings for the OJ attack (PIT, 2002) and the Improved OJ (IOJ, IEEE TIT 2025) attack, and obtain general and tight complexities on the RD, NHRD, and BRD problems. We show that the IOJ attack rests on optimistic assumptions that do not hold in practical random decoding scenarios, and thus its advantage over OJ should be disregarded in security assessments. For the RD problem, the OJ attack remains a strong candidate for the most powerful combinatorial attack in certain parameter regions, particularly when the code dimension $k$ is small and the extension
degree $m$ is large. For the NHRD problem, we show that the OJ attack is the most powerful combinatorial attack for the parameters of NH-Multi-UR-AG, yielding up to a 100-bit improvement over the adapted AGHT attack (IEEE TIT 2024), while still preserving the claimed security level. For the BRD problem, we derive complexity formulas for general block structures, resolving questions posed in prior works (Asiacrypt 2023, IEEE TIT 2025, PQC 2024). Our analysis also reveals that the OJ attack is previously underestimated by about $\gamma^2$ bits, where $\gamma$ denotes the minimum block weight.  We further show that the OJ attack outperforms AGHT and PRR attacks in certain parameter regions, achieving up to a 136-bit advantage over PRR (IEEE TIT 2025). Our work advances the understanding of decoding problems in the rank metrics and reinforces the security of related cryptosystems.

1 Introduction

Code-based cryptography is a promising candidate for post-quantum cryptogra-
phy. HQC [20] using Hamming metric codes recently has been selected by NIST
PQC for the final standardization [22]. As an alternative, rank-based cryptogra-
phy, namely code-based cryptography using rank metric codes, offers competi-
tive performance [21]. Recent works [8,2,28,1,26] further explored the potential
of rank metric cryptosystems, showing that McEliece, NTRU, Alekhnovich, and
MPCitHead approaches outperform the Hamming metric counterparts in band-
width. The typical cryptosystems are LowMS [2], ROLLO [28,1,26], RQC [28,1,26],
Multi-UR-AG [8,26], and RYDE [9,10,11], whose security relies on the hardness
of the rank decoding problems for Fqm -linear codes with rank metric.
Fqm -Linear Codes with Rank Metric. An Fqm -linear code ([n, k]qm -code)
with rank metric of length n and dimension k is a k-dimensional subspace of
Fnqm , which can be represented by a generator matrix of size k × n and rank k
over Fqm . For a fixed basis of Fqm , any vector in Fnqm has an associated matrix
in Fm×n
     q   . The rank weight of the vector is defined as the rank of its associated
matrix. The support is the Fq -linear subspace of Fqm spanned by its coordinates.
We call an error whose entries sharing a support a homogeneous (or standard)
error. Any error of weight r and length n is determined by two parts: the basis
(a vector in Frqm ) of its support and the representation (a matrix in Fr×n
                                                                        q   ) under
the basis. The associated matrix of the basis is called the support matrix and
the representation is called the coeﬀicient matrix.
The RD/NHRD/BRD Problems. The Rank Decoding (RD) problem is to
recover x and an error e from the noisy codeword y = xG + e, given a generator
matrix G of a random [n, k]qm -code. Recently, for designing eﬀicient cryptosys-
tems, two variants are proposed: the Non-Homogeneous RD (NHRD) problem
[19,8] and the Blockwise RD (BRD) problem [27,28]. The main difference con-
sists in the definition of the error e. In the NHRD problem, one solves a non-
homogeneous error, where an error is divided into three blocks whose first and
third blocks share a support included in the support of the second block. The
typical cryptosystems based on the NHRD problem are NH-Multi-RQC-AG and
NH-Multi-UR-AG [8], two eﬀicient encryptions. In the BRD problem, one solves
a blockwise error, where an error is divided into some blocks whose supports are
in direct sum. The BRD problem underlies blockwise RQC and ROLLO (BRQC
and BROLLO), obtaining more practical bandwidths.

Attacks and Limitations. All known attacks against the above decoding prob-
lems are exponential, thereby making them promising hard problems for secure
cryptosystems. The known attacks can be categorized into combinatorial at-
tacks and algebraic attacks. The algebraic attacks have been extensively studied
in recent years, with the Maximal Minors (MM) attack [4,6,5] emerging as the
most powerful approach for most cryptographic parameter sets. The algebraic
attacks typically determine the classical security level, since no direct quantum
speedup is known for such attacks [9,11]. The combinatorial attacks are various:
the Chabaud–Stern (CS) attack [14], the Ourivski-Johansson (OJ) attack [24],
the Gaborit-Ruat-Schrek (GRS) attack [16], and the Aragon-Gaborit-Hauteville-
Tillich (AGHT) attack [3]. For the NHRD and BRD problems, the tailored at-
tacks have been proposed, including AGHT-NHRD [8] for NHRD, as well as
Puchinger-Renner-Rosenkilde (PRR) [25] and Improved OJ (IOJ) [28] for BRD.
Before the introduction of the MM attack, combinatorial attacks were commonly
used to estimate both classical and quantum security of cryptosystems. Following
the advent of the MM attack, they are now primarily used to estimate quantum
security, typically by applying a quadratic speedup and dividing the exponential
complexity by a factor of 2. For various current cryptographic parameters, the
best combinatorial attack is not yet clearly identified. While the OJ and AGHT
attacks often outperform the CS and GRS attacks, their concrete advantages
are not always significant or well understood.
    The OJ-type attacks consist of two techniques: basis enumeration and coordi-
nate enumeration. Basis enumeration mainly guesses the support matrix, while
coordinate enumeration focuses on the coeﬀicient matrix. Unlike basis enumer-
ation, coordinate enumeration strongly depends on the structure of error and
becomes increasingly diﬀicult for structured errors. Overall, despite several re-
cent refinements [28,1] on the OJ-type attacks, the modeling, soundness, and
complexity analysis remain poorly understood, especially for structured decod-
ing problems such as NHRD and BRD. In particular, the interaction between
basis enumeration, coordinate enumeration, and structured errors has not been
systematically characterized, preventing the derivation of general and tight com-
plexity. This gap undermines confidence in quantum security and hinders the
design of compact schemes. RYDE’s [9,10,11] recent exclusion from the next
round of NIST PQC signature candidates [23] — partly due to the immature
complexity analysis of the underlying decoding variants — further motivates a
rigorous study of rank decoding.

1.1 Our Contributions
In this work, we develop a unified understanding of OJ-type attacks and their
applications to structured rank decoding problems, and reinforce the security of
related cryptosystems. Our main contributions are summarized as follows.
 – Unified (I)OJ modeling and tight complexity analysis. We refine the
   (I)OJ modeling techniques and derive general, and tight complexity esti-
   mates for the RD, NHRD, and BRD problems. We show that basis enumer-
   ation is independent of the error structure, whereas coordinate enumeration


                                       3
   fundamentally depends on the structure of error representations. Moreover,
   we demonstrate that the IOJ attack relies on overly optimistic assumptions,
   which limits its applicability in practical random decoding settings.
 – Improved understanding of OJ attacks on the RD problem. We de-
   rive a general complexity expression for the OJ attack on the RD problem for
   arbitrary code parameters. By our analysis, the OJ attack still has chance to
   outperform the AGHT attack and become the most powerful combinatorial
   attack for certain parameter regions, particularly those with small k and
   large m.
 – OJ attacks on the NHRD problem. We adapt the OJ attack to the
   NHRD problem and show that, for the parameter sets of NH-Multi-UR-
   AG [8], it becomes the most powerful known combinatorial attack. Compared
   with the AGHT-NHRD attack [8], the complexity improvement reaches up
   to 100 bits. Nevertheless, NH-Multi-UR-AG still remains within its claimed
   security level.
 – OJ attacks on the BRD problem and implications for sum-rank
   decoding. We derive general and tight complexity estimates for the OJ
   attack on the BRD problem with general block structures. We show that
   the OJ attack actually has higher complexity than the IOJ attack, with
   a gap of about γ 2 bits, where γ denotes the minimum block weight. For
   parameter regions with large m and small k, the OJ attack outperforms the
   AGHT and PRR attacks [28], thereby becoming the most powerful known
   combinatorial attack. For 256-bit secure BRQC instances, the complexity
   improvement over the PRR attack reaches up to 136 bits. Moreover, since
   blockwise errors are closely related to sum-rank metric errors [13,25,18], our
   analysis also advances the understanding of the OJ attack for decoding sum-
   rank codes.

1.2 Related Work
The Attacks on the RD Problem. There currently exist combinatorial at-
tacks [14,24,16,3] and algebraic attacks [16,4,6,5] on the RD problem. The al-
gebraic attacks resort to solve an algebraic system and the complexity is deter-
mined by the cost solving the system, specifically the number of unknowns and
linearly independent equations. The first algebraic attack is the AP attack [16]
exploiting annihilator polynomials. For current cryptographic parameters, this
attack is considered to be very ineﬀicient. A breakthrough algebraic attack is
proposed in [4], where the authors found that the Fqm -linearity is allowed to
devise a dedicated system, i.e., the Maximal Minors (MM) modeling. Then the
MM modeling is refined and improved in [6]. The resulting MM modeling subtly
reduces the RD problem to solving a linear system. This does not mean that the
RD problem can be eﬀiciently solved because the obtained system leads easily to
an underdetermined case or is very huge. The authors in [6] also found that one
can devise another algebraic system, i.e., the Support-Minors (SM) modeling,
by combining equations of the MM modeling. The SM modeling later is proven
to be too optimistic and underestimates the complexity since there exist a linear


                                       4
dependency between the SM modeling and the MM modeling [5]. By excluding
linear dependent equations, the authors obtained the SM-F+    q m modeling [5]. The
analysis in [5] shows that the cost of the SM-F+   q m modeling  is slightly large to
that of the MM modeling [6]. These two algebraic attacks are independent of
the size of q, can well exploit the structure of errors, and perform very powerful
for most parameter regions.
    The basic idea of the combinatorial attacks is to guess some unknowns about
the information of error, then solve a linear system such as a parity-check equa-
tion to check the correctness of guess with the unique-solution condition, gen-
erally the equations are more than the unknowns. The guess cost is the main
complexity for the combinatorial attacks. The first combinatorial attack is the
CS attack proposed in [14]. Later, the CS attack was significantly improved
in [24] by Ourivski and Johansson, namely the OJ attack. After 14 years, a new
combinatorial attack was found, the GRS attack [16]. In 2018, Aragon, Gaborit,
Hauteville, and Tillich further refined the GRS attack and proposed a new im-
provement, namely the AGHT attack [3]. The CS, GRS, and AGHT attacks
consist of subtly guessing the support of the error then solving the parity-check
equation to check the correctness of guessing. The OJ attack [24] transforms the
quadratic multivariate system about the entries of support/coeﬀicient matrices
into a linear system. For currently most cryptographic parameters, the OJ and
AGHT attacks are powerful combinatorial attacks. The former benefits from
the small k and the latter from a small m and rate k/n. However, the underly-
ing modelings remain insuﬀiciently understood. This lack of understanding may
weaken confidence in the security of the corresponding cryptosystems and hin-
der the identification of more compact parameter sets for eﬀicient cryptographic
constructions. One can observe that, while the works [4,6] exploit the underlying
idea of the OJ attack to build the MM attack, they do not provide a general
modeling for the OJ attack, nor do they elaborate on the basis/coordinate enu-
meration techniques.
The Attacks on the NHRD Problem. In [8], the authors introduce the
NHRD problem and construct two cryptosystems, namely NH-Multi-RQC-AG
and NH-Multi-UR-AG. To estimate the security of cryptosystems, they adapt
the MM attack and the AGHT attack. We denote the adapted AGHT attack
by AGHT-NHRD. This attack is regarded as the most powerful combinatorial
attack for the NHRD problem. However, the impact of AGHT-NHRD appears
to vary across different parameter regions of the two cryptosystems. In partic-
ular, for NH-Multi-UR-AG, the dimension parameter of the underlying NHRD
instance is relatively small, which suggests that the OJ attack may become ap-
plicable and potentially more powerful than AGHT-NHRD. This indicates that
the security of NHRD should also be evaluated with respect to the OJ attack.
Nevertheless, adapting the OJ attack to the NHRD problem is non-trivial.
The Attacks on the BRD Problem. In addition to the SM modeling, typical
combinatorial and algebraic attacks on the RD problem have been adapted to
the BRD problem in [27,1,28,26]. In [28], the authors further adapt the PRR
attack [25] for decoding sum-rank codes to the BRD problem. More recently,


                                         5
the MM attack has been refined to obtain a more precise and general com-
plexity analysis by deriving tight upper bounds on the number of independent
equations across general block structures [26]. Regarding the OJ attack [24], the
works [27,1,28] in fact give a refinement of the original framework. To distin-
guish it from the original OJ attack, we refer to this variant as the IOJ attack.
However, several issues remain unresolved for the IOJ attack. Its soundness has
not been fully established, and its complexity has only been analyzed for spe-
cial cases—typically two or three equal‑length blocks—rather than for general
block structures. In particular, for structured errors such as blockwise errors,
their representations typically exhibit specific algebraic structures, which make
coordinate enumeration highly non-trivial and hinder the derivation of a gen-
eral complexity expression. These issues stem from a limited understanding of
the underlying (I)OJ modeling and the associated basis/coordinate enumeration
techniques. Addressing these challenges requires a refined (I)OJ modeling for the
BRD problem, together with a tight complexity over general block structures.


1.3 Organization

Section 2 presents notations and preliminaries. To derive the tight complexity
for the OJ attack, Section 3 reduces the standard/non-homogeneous/blockwise
errors. Section 4 refines the (I)OJ modeling and shows that the IOJ attack can
be avoided. Sections 5, 6, and 7 respectively derive the complexity of the OJ
attack against the RD/NHRD/BRD problems and obtain general and compact
complexity expressions. We conclude this paper in Section 8.
